passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments, according to Sheminith. A Psalm of David” (verse 1).

The prayer begins with fear: “O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath” (verse 1). Then a plea: “Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are in agony” (verse 2).

“My soul is deeply distressed. How long, O LORD, how long?” (verse 3). The sentence breaks off. He cannot finish it.

He begs God to turn back to him: “Turn, O LORD, and deliver my soul; save me because of Your loving devotion” (verse 4). And he gives a reason: “For there is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol?” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Sheminith means ‘the eighth’ in Hebrew. It may name an eight-stringed instrument, a lower range of voice, or a tune. No one knows for certain. It appears again in Psalm 12's heading and in 1 Chronicles 15:21.

The man is ill, or in such distress that his whole body aches. ‘My bones are in agony’ means the pain has reached the deepest part of him. ‘Soul’ is the Hebrew nephesh: not a ghostly part of a person, but the whole living self. ‘My soul is deeply distressed’ means: I am shaken through and through.

Many in Israel, as in the whole ancient world, assumed that sickness was a sign of God's anger. That is why he begins, ‘do not rebuke me in Your anger.’ Notice that the psalm never says he has sinned, and never says God sent the illness to punish him. Scripture argues against reading every illness that way, at length in the book of Job, and Jesus did too (John 9:2-3).

‘How long?’ is the cry of the lament psalms. It is not a polite question. It is a complaint brought straight to God by someone who believes God is there and ought to act.

‘Loving devotion’ is hesed, God's faithful, promised love. He does not appeal to his own goodness. He appeals to God's.

Sheol is the Hebrew name for the place of the dead, pictured as dark and silent, below the earth. Verse 5 is the man's argument with God: if I die, one voice that praises you goes quiet.
passages.later:
King Hezekiah, sick to the point of death, prayed in almost the same words: “For Sheol cannot thank You; Death cannot praise You” (Isaiah 38:18). Psalm 30 argues the same way: “Will the dust praise You?” (Psalm 30:9).

In John's Gospel, as his death drew near, Jesus said, “Now My soul is troubled” (John 12:27). Some readers hear an echo of verse 3.

Hebrews says that Jesus himself “offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death” (Hebrews 5:7). The one who prays Psalm 6 is not praying alone.

Later the Bible speaks more plainly of life beyond death: “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19), and “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake” (Daniel 12:2).
passages.hard:
‘In death there is no remembrance of You’, as some Bibles put verse 5. Did the psalmist believe in life after death?

Many psalmists do not seem to know of a happy life with God after death. Sheol is pictured as silence. Their hope is rescue from dying now, so they can go on praising God among the living. Other lines in the Psalms reach further (16:10; 49:15; 73:24), and later the Old Testament speaks plainly of the dead rising (Daniel 12:2). The book page on the Psalms sets out how readers weigh these lines, in the part on Sheol.

Notice what verse 5 is doing. It is not a lesson about the afterlife. It is a man arguing with God for his life. And notice that the Bible does not treat death as natural or good. It treats death as an enemy. For Christians the fuller answer comes with the rising of Jesus from the dead.

There is a second hard thing here. Psalm 6 is one of the church's seven ‘penitential psalms’, prayers of sorrow for sin (with 32, 38, 51, 102, 130 and 143), a grouping known from the sixth century. Yet this psalm confesses no sin. It is right to pray it in repentance. It is just as right to pray it when you are suffering and have done nothing to deserve it.
passages.asks:
Psalm 6 gives you permission to say ‘How long?’ to God and not finish the sentence. That is prayer too.

If you are ill or in pain, this is a psalm you can pray as it is, without dressing it up.

passages.t: ‘I flood my bed with weeping’, and ‘The LORD has heard’
passages.happening:
The man describes his nights. “I am weary from groaning; all night I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears” (verse 6). “My eyes fail from grief; they grow dim because of all my foes” (verse 7).

Then, all at once, the psalm turns. “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard my weeping” (verse 8). “The LORD has heard my cry for mercy; the LORD accepts my prayer” (verse 9).

It ends, “All my enemies will be ashamed and dismayed; they will turn back in sudden disgrace” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
‘Flood my bed’ and ‘drench my couch’ are not exaggeration for its own sake. Hebrew poetry uses large pictures to tell the truth about pain. Night after night, the man cannot stop weeping.

‘My eyes fail’ means they grow weak and dim from crying. His enemies make it worse. In a world that read sickness as God's anger, a sick man's enemies could say God was against him.

The turn in verse 8 is sudden. Nothing in the psalm says what changed. Some readers think a priest or another worshipper spoke a word of comfort to him between verses 7 and 8. Others think the change came inside him as he prayed. The psalm does not say whether he was healed yet. It says he was heard.

Notice that his weeping itself is called a prayer. ‘The LORD has heard my weeping.’ The tears were not a failure of faith. God received them.

‘Turn back’ in verse 10 is the same Hebrew word as ‘turn’ in verse 4. He asked God to turn to him; now his enemies turn away.
passages.later:
Jesus uses the words of verse 8 in Matthew. On the last day, he says, he will tell false followers, “depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness” (Matthew 7:23). In Luke he says, “Depart from me, all you evildoers” (Luke 13:27).

Another psalm says, “Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning” (Psalm 30:5). And Revelation promises a day when God “will wipe away every tear from their eyes” and there will be “no more death or mourning or crying or pain” (Revelation 21:4).

In Gethsemane Jesus said, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death” (Matthew 26:38). The Son of God knew nights like this.
passages.hard:
Does this psalm mean that if you pray hard enough, the weeping will stop at once? No. The psalm moves from tears to trust within ten verses, but it does not say how long the nights lasted. Many laments turn like this one; Psalm 88 never turns at all, and God kept it in the Bible too. A prayer may end in the dark, and the person whose grief has not lifted is not praying wrong.

Nor does Psalm 6 say that the man lacked faith because he wept. He wept, and he prayed, and the weeping was part of the prayer. Lament is not unbelief. You do not argue with a God you have given up on.

The psalm does not give his sorrow a medical name, and these notes do not give anyone's sorrow a name either. But if your nights are like the nights in this psalm, please do not carry them alone. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor, or a friend. When grief or sadness lasts and starts taking sleep, appetite or work, seeing a doctor is wise, and it is not a failure of faith. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, please speak to someone now: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
The psalm lets you weep before God and calls the weeping prayer. Ask whether you have hidden your tears from God, as if they were not allowed.

You can pray this psalm for yourself, or for someone you love who cannot pray it tonight. ‘The LORD has heard my weeping’ is a sentence worth saying aloud, even before you feel it.
